blocks.text: Binary trees come in a few named shapes. The names show up constantly — in interview questions ("check whether a tree is complete"), in data structures (a heap is a *complete* tree), and in complexity arguments ("in a *balanced* tree this is O(log n)"). Here are the ones worth knowing, and the counting facts that come with them.

blocks.alt: Five shapes. Full: every node has 0 or 2 children. Complete: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left. Perfect: every level is completely full. Balanced: at every node the two subtree heights differ by at most 1. Degenerate: every node has one child, forming a chain.

items: **Full** (or *proper*) — every node has **0 or 2** children. No node has just one.
**Complete** — every level is completely filled **except possibly the last**, and the last level is filled **from the left** with no gaps. In the level-order array, no node ever appears after a null.
**Perfect** — every internal node has two children **and** every leaf is at the same depth. It is both full and complete, with exactly 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.
**Balanced** (height-balanced) — at **every** node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. This keeps the height O(log n).
**Degenerate** (or *skewed*) — every node has at most one child, so the tree is really a linked list with height n − 1.

blocks.text: And one that is about **values**, not shape: a **binary search tree** keeps everything in a node's left subtree smaller and everything in its right subtree bigger (previous lesson). A BST can have any of the shapes above — and its speed depends on which one.

All three of full, complete and perfect fall out of one level-order walk. **Full**: no node has exactly one child. **Complete**: walk the child slots in level order — once you've seen an empty slot, you must never see a real node again. **Perfect**: complete, and the node count is 2^k − 1 for some k.

blocks.text: **O(n) time, O(w) space** for the queue, where w is the widest level.
Complete trees fit in an array

A complete tree has no gaps, so it can be stored in a plain array in level order — no pointers at all. The children and parent of index i are found by arithmetic. This is exactly how a **heap** (priority queue) is stored.

blocks.alt: A complete tree with values 10 to 60 at indexes 0 to 5, and the same values in an array. The node at index 1 has children at indexes 3 and 4, which are 2 times 1 plus 1 and 2 times 1 plus 2; its parent is index 0, (1 minus 1) divided by 2.

elements.text:
children of i:  2i + 1  and  2i + 2
parent of i:    (i - 1) / 2, rounded down
elements.originalText:
children of i:  2i + 1  and  2i + 2
parent of i:    (i - 1) / 2, rounded down

blocks.alt: Six facts. Level L holds at most 2 to the power L nodes. A perfect tree of height h has 2 to the power h plus 1, minus 1, nodes. n nodes need a height of at least floor of log base 2 of n. A tree with n nodes has n minus 1 edges. It has n plus 1 empty child pointers. In a full tree, leaves equal internal nodes plus 1.

level L holds at most              2^L nodes
a perfect tree of height h has     2^(h+1) - 1 nodes
n nodes need a height of at least  floor(log2 n)
n nodes are joined by              n - 1 edges

in a full tree:                    leaves = internal nodes + 1

blocks.text: The third fact is why balanced trees are fast: you can't fit n nodes into fewer than about log₂ n levels, and a balanced tree stays close to that minimum. The fourth and fifth are handy sanity checks: every node except the root has exactly one incoming edge, and each of the n nodes has 2 child slots, of which n − 1 are used.

items: **Full**: 0 or 2 children. **Complete**: no gaps in level order. **Perfect**: every level full.
**Balanced**: subtree heights differ by ≤ 1 everywhere, so height stays O(log n). **Degenerate**: a chain, height n − 1.
A complete tree can live in an array: children of i at **2i + 1** and **2i + 2** — the layout of a heap.
Level L holds ≤ 2^L nodes; n nodes have n − 1 edges and need height ≥ ⌊log₂ n⌋.
